title: Return to Sport and Clinical Outcomes after Surgical Stabilization of Chronic Ankle Instability in Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) can compromise athletic performance and delay return to competition. Although primary ligament repair and ligament reconstruction are valid surgical options, comparative data remains limited.
PURPOSE: The primary aim was to evaluate overall return-to-sport outcomes after surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability in athletes. The secondary aim was to compare return-to-sport and postoperative clinical outcomes between direct ligament repair and ligament reconstruction.
STUDY DESIGN: Comparative retrospective study METHODS: This comparative cohort study included 54 athletes who underwent surgical stabilization for CAI between 2018 and 2024. Surgical procedures were categorized as primary repair and ligament reconstruction. The primary outcomes were RTS status and time to RTS. Secondary outcomes included postoperative Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) scores and residual complaints.
RESULTS: The mean age was 25.6 ± 6.9 years, and 48% of patients were football players. The median interval from the latest injury to surgery was 6.0 months. RTS status was available for 49 of the 54 athletes (91%). Of these, 48 (98%) returned to sport at a mean time of 5.3 months (range 2.0 to 16.0), while one athlete did not return to sport. Postoperative functional outcomes were favorable, with mean FAAM activities of daily living and sport scores of 96.2 ± 8.3 and 89.7 ± 20.4, respectively. No statistically significant differences were observed among surgical groups in RTS status, time to RTS, FAAM scores, or residual complaints.
CONCLUSION: Surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability was associated with favorable postoperative scores and a high RTS rate among athletes with available outcome data. The sample size and overall study design preclude conclusions regarding the equivalence or superiority of repair versus reconstruction.

title: Relationship between global functional outcomes and patient-reported instability after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction: A midterm case series of 292 patients.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate midterm patient-reported outcomes, return to sport (RTS) rates and instability-specific symptoms after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction (AALALR), and to evaluate the relationship between global functional recovery and perceived ankle stability.
METHODS: We retrospectively analysed 292 patients who underwent AALALR between January 2015 and May 2022, with a mean follow-up of 4.9 ± 1.8 years. Global outcomes were assessed using the foot and ankle ability measure (FAAM) and simple ankle value (SAV), while instability-specific perception was evaluated with the French Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT-F). RTS, satisfaction and complications were also recorded. No objective postoperative laxity assessment was performed.
RESULTS: Mean FAAM-ADL was 94.3 ± 12.0, FAAM-Sports 87.5 ± 20.4 and SAV 85.1 ± 17.4; 89.7% of patients returned to sport and 91.1% were satisfied. Overall, 104 patients (35.6%; 95% CI, 30.3-41.3) met the CAIT-F criterion for instability at follow-up (score ≤23/30). Patients with CAIT-F-defined instability had significantly lower FAAM and SAV scores and RTS rates (all p < 0.001), although most had returned to sport (79.8%) and were satisfied (81.7%). The CAIT-F correlated moderately with FAAM-activities of daily living (ADL), FAAM-Sports and SAV (Spearman ρ = 0.68-0.69) and receiver operating characteristic analysis showed imperfect agreement between global scores and CAIT-F-defined categories (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.82-0.85). The reoperation rate was 5.5%.
CONCLUSION: AALALR provides high midterm satisfaction, favourable functional scores and favourable RTS rates. However, over one-third of patients reported current CAIT-F-defined instability symptoms. Global and instability-specific instruments are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable, and prospective studies including objective laxity assessment are needed.

title: Indications, Techniques, and Outcomes of Meniscus Centralization for Root Tears and Meniscus Transplantation: An International Expert Consensus Statement.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop an expert consensus statement on the biomechanics, diagnosis, surgical indications and techniques, rehabilitation protocols, and postoperative outcomes of centralization procedures in meniscus root pathology and meniscal allograft transplantation.
METHODS: A working group generated 39 statements on meniscal centralization from previously published data for evaluation in a 3-round modified Delphi process. A panel of 22 international experts rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale, and statements were retained, revised, or excluded according to predefined thresholds (≥75% agreement and <20% disagreement). Rounds 1 and 2 included both literature-derived items and open-ended responses, allowing panel members to propose additional statements.
RESULTS: Ultimately, 35 statements were retained, with 100% participation across all rounds. The expert panel reached consensus that centralization may be considered in the setting of root repair and meniscal allograft transplantation to reduce meniscal extrusion (ME), improve joint contact mechanics, potentially enhance root healing, and limit displacement of the repair. The expert panel suggested that the degree of ME may help guide decision-making and that successful outcomes after medial meniscus posterior root repair with centralization may be evaluated by changes in ME and degenerative progression. Medial meniscus posterior root centralization should be considered when ME on magnetic resonance imaging exceeds 3 mm, and lateral centralization should be considered for lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and >3 mm extrusion. Centralization was not recommended in advanced osteoarthritis. Panelists supported its use in symptomatic medial ME with varus deformity in combination with high tibial osteotomy. Transtibial tunnels, suture anchors, and hybrid constructs were all considered acceptable, provided that fixation is individualized to the location of ME and native meniscotibial anatomy and overtightening is avoided. The panel emphasized the need for long-term studies to confirm the durability and joint-protective benefits of centralization.
CONCLUSIONS: The panel supported consideration of meniscal centralization when magnetic resonance imaging shows extrusion greater than 3 mm in medial meniscus posterior root tears and in selected lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and extrusion greater than 3 mm. Its use was discouraged in the setting of advanced osteoarthritis, whereas a combined approach with high tibial osteotomy was supported in patients with symptomatic varus-associated medial ME. No single fixation construct was preferred; transtibial, anchor-based, and hybrid techniques were all considered acceptable. Emphasis was placed on individualized surgical decision-making and on avoiding overconstraint.

title: Patients treated with rehabilitation alone after anterior cruciate ligament injury display greater muscle strength symmetry, yet lower absolute muscle strength normalized to bodyweight compared to reconstruction: A Cross-sectional study of 3,093 patients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Younger patients active at a greater activity level are in general treated with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) while older, less active patients receive rehabilitation alone as primary treatment. Objective of this study was to compare muscle strength, and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) between patients treated with rehabilitation alone and rehabilitation with additional ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during the first 12 months after treatment.
DESIGN: Registry-based cohort study.
SETTING: Cross-sectional comparisons adjusted for age and sex using ANCOVA.
PARTICIPANTS: 3093 patients (2707 ACLR; 386 rehabilitation), aged ≥15 years and registered in Project ACL.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Muscle strength and PROs assessed at 10 weeks, 4, 8, and 12 months after ACL injury or ACLR.
RESULTS: In the comparison between patients treated with rehabilitation alone and ACLR, patients in the rehabilitation alone group had greater muscle strength symmetry at all follow-ups but lower absolute strength normalized to bodyweight in the uninjured limb, except hamstrings strength at 10 weeks. Patients in the rehabilitation group reported higher KOOS symptoms at 8- and 12 months and sports/recreation at 10 weeks, present K-SES18 was higher at 10 weeks but lower at 12 months, while future K-SES18 was lower at all follow-ups. Patients in the rehabilitation alone group reported lower ACL-RSI was lower at 12 months and Tegner activity levels were lower pre-injury and at all follow-ups.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients treated with rehabilitation alone had greater symmetrical strength, but lower uninjured limb absolute strength normalized to bodyweight compared to patients treated with ACLR. Patients in the rehabilitation alone group also reported less knee symptoms, but inferior present and future knee self-efficacy compared with patients treated with ACLR.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Long-term market value decline after medial collateral ligament injury in professional football players did not differ statistically significantly from matched non-injured controls: A Transfermarkt-based cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to characterize the longitudinal trajectory of estimated market value after medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury in professional football players and determine whether postinjury changes differed from matched non-injured controls.
METHODS: Professional football players with a recorded MCL injury were identified from Transfermarkt injury records labeled as medial (collateral) ligament injuries (seasons 2007/08-2023/24); duplicate records of the same episode were merged, and injuries were not clinically verified. Market value was assessed during the season preceding injury (Tpre), the injury season (T0), and annually for five subsequent seasons (T1-T5). Linear mixed-effect models evaluated longitudinal changes and associations with age, playing position, league level, and injury-related absence. Segmented models assessed changes in temporal trajectory. MCL cases were also matched 1:2 to non-injured controls by competition, season, playing position, age, and preinjury market value, with group differences examined using a difference-in-differences model.
RESULTS: Forty-five players with 50 MCL injury episodes were included, 8 of which had an associated anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal lesion. Median age at injury was 26.5 years (interquartile range [IQR]: 23.0-28.7), and median time lost was 42 days (IQR: 21-76.5). In the adjusted model, market value did not differ statistically significantly from Tpre at T0 (P = 0.649), T1 (P = 0.813), or T2 (P = 0.064) but was statistically significantly lower at T3 (-34.25%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -51.21% to -11.38%; P = 0.006), T4 (-47.54%; 95% CI: -61.54% to -28.43%; P < 0.001), and T5 (-51.70%; 95% CI: -65.25% to -32.88%; P < 0.001). No statistically significant postinjury change in slope was observed (P = 0.103). Thirty-one of 48 eligible cases were matched to 62 controls; the remaining 17 had no eligible control within the matching criteria, mostly because of lower-tier competition or low preinjury market value. Difference-in-differences estimates were not statistically significant at any time point (P = 0.167-0.561; range: -10.9% [95% CI: -39.2% to 30.6%] at T0 to -24.6% [95% CI: -49.5% to 12.6%] at T3); the study could detect only differences of approximately 42%-46% or more. Results were unchanged when analyses were restricted to isolated MCL injuries.
CONCLUSIONS: Market value declined substantially during long-term follow-up after MCL injury, but this decline was not statistically significantly different from that observed in matched non-injured players (P = 0.167-0.561). Much of the apparent long-term depreciation may therefore reflect the underlying age- and career-related trajectory of professional footballers; however, the matched analysis was underpowered, and a modest injury-specific effect, particularly after more severe injuries with longer absence, cannot be excluded. Because injury grade and treatment were unavailable, these findings should not be generalized to high-grade or operatively treated MCL injuries.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
abstract: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

title: Mid-term functional outcomes and graft survivorship after allograft ACL reconstruction in recreationally active adults aged 40-60 years.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: An increasing proportion of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstructions are performed in older recreationally active adults; however, mid-term functional and graft survivorship data remain limited for this specific population.
PURPOSE: To evaluate mid-term functional outcomes, return to recreational sport, and graft survivorship following primary allograft ACL reconstruction in recreationally active adults aged 40-60 years.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study included 300 recreationally active adults aged 40-60 years who underwent primary allograft ACL reconstruction between 2015 and 2019. All grafts were non-irradiated and preserved by freezing according to the tissue bank protocol. Validated patient-reported outcome measures (IKDC, KOOS, Tegner) were collected preoperatively and at final follow-up. Return to sport was defined as sustained participation in pre-injury recreational activity. Graft failure was defined by recurrent instability, imaging-confirmed rupture, or revision surgery. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess graft survivorship.
RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 62.4 ± 9.1 months, significant improvements were observed across all functional outcome measures. The mean IKDC score improved from 46.2 ± 11.8 preoperatively to 82.4 ± 10.6 at final follow-up, and the mean KOOS overall score increased from 58.7 ± 13.4 to 86.1 ± 9.8. Documented resumption of recreational sport participation occurred in 87.3% of patients at a mean of 8.9 ± 2.4 months postoperatively. Kaplan-Meier graft survivorship was 98.3% at 2 years, 96.7% at 3 years, and 94.8% at 5 years. Sixteen graft failures (5.3%) were recorded.
CONCLUSION: In recreationally active adults aged 40-60 years, primary allograft ACL reconstruction was associated with improvement in patient-reported outcomes, frequent resumption of recreational sport participation, and satisfactory graft survivorship at mid-term follow-up.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are more frequent in female football players, but sex-specific differences in injury characteristics remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to analyse sex-specific differences in ACL injury incidence and characteristics in professional football.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study used data from a German national ACL registry ('Kreuzbandregister im Deutschen Fußball'), including professional male (first to third league) and female (first and second league) football players from the 2016/2017 to 2024/2025 seasons. Incidence rates were compared using Poisson regression (incidence rate ratio, IRR) and injury characteristics using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: A total of 459 ACL injuries were analysed (177 female and 282 male). The rate was 1.19 versus 0.69 per 1000 match hours (IRR 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.13). The difference was most pronounced in the first division (IRR 2.49, 1.82-3.41) and smaller and not significant in the lower leagues (IRR 1.24, 0.93-1.65). Injuries in female players were more often non-contact (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.37) and indirect-contact injuries (aOR 2.92), occurred more often on artificial turf (aOR 5.42) and in national team players (aOR 3.03). Concomitant injury patterns did not differ significantly, except for fewer lateral collateral ligament injuries in women.
CONCLUSION: ACL injury rates are higher in female professional football players, particularly in the first division. The predominance of non-contact and indirect-contact mechanisms supports targeted, sex-specific prevention strategies.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

title: Lower Sport Nutrition Knowledge in Masters Track and Field Athletes Compared with Younger Competitors.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Appropriate nutrition is essential for supporting both athletic performance and healthy aging. In masters athletes, the physiological demands of aging and the nutritional needs of competitive sport are combined. However, dietary intakes of masters athletes do not generally meet sport nutrition recommendations. Despite evidence linking nutrition knowledge to dietary quality, sport nutrition knowledge among competitive masters athletes has not previously been evaluated.
OBJECTIVES: The primary objective of this observational cross-sectional study was to assess nutrition knowledge in masters athletes competing at the World Masters Athletics Championships compared to varsity athletes with structured dietetic support.
METHODS: Masters track and field athletes competing at World Masters Athletics Championships as well as varsity university track and field athletes completed the Abridged Nutrition for Sport Knowledge Questionnaire to assess both general and sport-specific nutritional knowledge. Differences in scores attained by masters and varsity athletes were assessed using independent t-tests.
RESULTS: A total of 238 athletes participated (n=86 varsity athletes; n=152 masters athletes; n=120 males; n=118 females). Varsity athletes scored significantly higher on overall nutrition knowledge (51.0±12.8%) compared with masters athletes (45.2±15.0%; p=0.002). Varsity athletes also demonstrated higher scores in general nutrition (p=0.02), sport nutrition (p=0.01), and carbohydrate-related knowledge (p=0.01). No statistically significant differences were observed between groups for protein-related knowledge (p=0.09). A significant main effect of sex was observed for knowledge relating to protein, with males scoring higher than females (43.0±21.5% vs. 38.5±21.6%; p=0.039).
CONCLUSIONS: Masters athletes demonstrated lower nutrition knowledge compared to varsity athletes across general and sport specific domains, with particular deficits observed in questions pertaining to carbohydrates. Given the nutritional needs of aging athletes, these gaps may contribute to the documented disconnect between dietary intake and recommendations. Tailored, evidence-based nutrition education may help improve dietary behaviors, training adaptations, and long-term health outcomes in masters athletes.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

title: [Research progress on correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament injury and bone bruise].
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To review the research progress on the correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and bone bruise.
METHODS: Relevant literature on non-contact ACL injury and bone bruise published in recent years was reviewed. The imaging characteristics and injury mechanisms of bone bruise, factors affecting bone bruise distribution, the associations between bone bruise and combined intra-articular injuries, and the impact of bone bruise on postoperative outcomes after ACL reconstruction were summarized and analyzed.
RESULTS: Bone bruise is a common MRI finding in non-contact ACL injury, mainly involving the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau. The typical "kissing" bone bruise pattern can reflect the abnormal loading condition of the knee joint at the moment of injury and provides important imaging evidence for inferring the injury mechanism of ACL rupture. The occurrence and distribution of bone bruise may be influenced by factors such as age, osseous morphology of the knee, and meniscal anatomical characteristics. The extent, location, and severity of bone bruise are associated with knee laxity, anterolateral ligament injury, meniscal tears, and articular cartilage injury to varying degrees. Among these, the association between lateral compartment bone bruise and lateral meniscal injury is relatively well established, while bone bruise of the medial tibial plateau may indicate occult posterior horn injury of the medial meniscus. Bone bruise may also be associated with early postoperative pain and recovery of knee range of motion after ACL reconstruction, and may increase the risk of cartilage degeneration and post-traumatic osteoarthritis. However, its predictive value for mid- and long-term knee function and clinical outcomes remains inconclusive.
CONCLUSION: Bone bruise can reflect, to some extent, the loading mechanism and severity of non-contact ACL injury, and provides important clues for identifying associated structural injuries and evaluating prognosis. However, the grading and assessment criteria for bone bruise remain unstandardized, and controversies remain regarding its associations with certain combined injuries and long-term clinical outcomes. Further standardized, large-scale, multi-center, and long-term follow-up studies are required to clarify the clinical value of bone bruise in the assessment and prognostic evaluation of ACL injury.

title: Most National Football League Players Return to Play After Achilles Tendon Repair, Yet Only One-Half Regain Preinjury Performance With Persistent Pass-Rush Decline at Year 2.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate National Football League (NFL) player performance using advanced statistics after Achilles tendon (AT) repair.
METHODS: NFL players who underwent AT repair between 2017 and 2023 were identified from a publicly available injury database. Demographic and performance data were collected preinjury and up to 2 seasons postinjury, with a minimum follow-up of 1 regular-season game required to assess return to play (RTP). RTP was defined as being active for a regular-season game and return to performance as achieving ≥90% of preinjury performance. Performance was assessed using Sports Information Solutions' points above replacement (PAR). Factors associated with RTP and return to performance were analyzed using binary logistic regression, with pre- and postinjury performance compared using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate.
RESULTS: Seventy-seven NFL players with AT repairs were identified. Ten were excluded for no prior regular-season play, leaving 67 included. Overall, 77.6% (n = 52) returned to play. Increasing age reduced the odds of RTP (odds ratio 0.75, 95% confidence interval [0.60-0.95], P = .02). Index games preinjury increased the odds of RTP (odds ratio 1.12, 95% confidence interval [1.01-1.24], P = .04). Body mass index, position, index games played, and index PAR were not significant. Among returnees, 50% (n = 26) achieved at least 90% of preinjury performance. Higher index PAR predicted lower odds of meeting this threshold (odds ratio 0.77, 95% confidence interval [0.66-0.90], P = .00). Pass-rush PAR declined at year 2 after injury from 1.17 (±5.19) preinjury to -0.66 (±2.15), P = .02.
CONCLUSIONS: In this study using publicly available data, 77.6% of NFL players returned to play after AT repair; however, only one-half of these players regained ≥90% of their preinjury performance. Older age reduced the likelihood of RTP, whereas more preinjury games started increased it. Higher preinjury PAR reduced the likelihood of performance recovery. Pass-rush performance declined by the second postinjury season.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective therapeutic case series.

title: From suspension to clearance: return-to-fight decision-making after concussion and knockout in combat sports-a critical review.
abstract: Combat-sport medical suspensions restrict participation after knockout, head-blow stoppage, or suspected concussion. Expiry of a suspension does not establish clinical recovery or replace required medical clearance. This critical narrative review examines how suspension rules, concussion care, and graded return to training can be coordinated in boxing and related combat sports. We critically integrated international concussion consensus, combat-sport guidance, official regulations, and selected rehabilitation and epidemiological studies. The reviewed guidance already combines time restrictions with medical requirements; differences concern duration, permitted activities, assessment criteria, and implementation. General concussion principles apply irrespective of whether the injury-producing contact was intentional. Early light physical activity and prescribed aerobic exercise must be distinguished from later sport-specific activity and renewed head-impact risk. We propose a framework with three dimensions-clinical recovery, regulatory eligibility, and functional progression-and three decision gates. Gate A is medical authorization for activity carrying head-impact risk; Gate B is expiry of the applicable no-contact restriction. Both are prerequisites for contact progression. Gate C permits competition only after the required training progression, expiry of the competition suspension, and final medical authorization. Clinicians determine medical readiness; coaches and rehabilitation staff support graded training within those limits. The dimensions may overlap, but contact progression follows Gates A and B and competition follows Gate C. Priorities are clearer activity definitions, consistent documentation of clearance, adherence to existing requirements, longitudinal records, and prospective evaluation. This framework is an unvalidated implementation proposal rather than a new clearance test or a universal suspension timetable.

title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized.
METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions.
RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.

title: Thumb muscle activation with task-specific exercise: A pilot study with participant self-report implementation outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis is a common source of pain, weakness, and reduced hand function and upper extremity rehabilitation. Although isometric stabilization exercises are commonly used in hand therapy to support dynamic thumb carpometacarpal control, limited task-specific evidence guides exercise selection.
PURPOSE: To examine muscle activation across four isometric thumb-hand positions in healthy adults and describe participant perceptions of the protocol's acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness before testing in symptomatic hand therapy samples.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional, within-subject repeated-measures pilot study.
METHODS: Seven healthy right-handed adults (mean age, 22.7 ± 0.48 years) performed four submaximal isometric exercise conditions at approximately 80% perceived effort: composite finger-thumb squeeze, "bunny-ears" pinch, resisted index-finger abduction, and fingertip-only press. Surface electromyography was recorded from the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, first dorsal interosseous, and forearm flexor group. Integrated electromyography was normalized within participants to each muscle's maximum response across conditions. A two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (condition × muscle) compared normalized activation. Participants rated acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness on five-point Likert scales.
RESULTS: Normalized activation differed by muscle, F(3,18) = 14.22, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.70, with a significant condition × muscle interaction, F(9,54) = 7.29, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55. Abductor pollicis brevis activation was highest during composite squeeze and bunny-ears pinch (0.93 ± 0.05 and 0.85 ± 0.06) and lowest during resisted index-finger abduction (0.31 ± 0.07). Opponens pollicis activation was highest during composite squeeze and resisted index-finger abduction (0.79 ± 0.07 and 0.75 ± 0.09). Mean construct-based ratings of acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ranged from 4.54-4.79 out of 5.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings provide preliminary evidence to inform hand therapy exercise selection by showing that functional isometric thumb-hand positions produce distinct intrinsic and extrinsic activation profiles. Favorable participant perceptions support protocol refinement and testing in larger and symptomatic hand therapy samples.

title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

title: Lower extremity joint biomechanics from a single crossover drop task demonstrate superior predictive potential for secondary ACL injuries than drop vertical jump or single leg landing tasks.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Secondary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries remain a significant concern after return-to-sport (RTS) following ACL reconstruction (ACLR), with rates as high as 24%. Identifying biomechanical predictors of re-injury is critical for improving RTS protocols.
PURPOSE: To compare the predictive potential of three common landing tasks [drop vertical jump (DVJ), single-leg landing (SLL), and single-leg crossover drop (SCD)] for secondary ACL injury risk in post-ACLR athletes.
METHODS: A multicenter cohort of 150 athletes (age 13-30 years) that were cleared for RTS post-ACLR completed DVJ, SLL, and SCD tasks during 3D motion analysis; 144 athletes data met criteria for analysis. Peak kinematic and kinetic variables (n = 126) were analyzed using a penalized logistic regression with an elastic net penalty. Predictive models were evaluated via ROC curves, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values.
RESULTS: The SCD task demonstrated the strongest predictive performance for secondary ACL injury, with a validated positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.57, negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.96, sensitivity of 80.0%, specificity of 88.9%, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.933. The DVJ demonstrated moderate predictive performance (PPV=0.43, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=85.7%, AUC=0.843), while the SLL demonstrated the lowest performance (PPV=0.33, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=78.6%, AUC=0.736).
CONCLUSION: Lower extremity biomechanics during SCD provide greater predictive performance for secondary ACL injury compared with the DVJ or SLL. The findings suggest that SCD captures biomechanical characteristics relevant to secondary ACL injury risk and may improve identification of athletes at elevated risk following ACL reconstruction. However, further validation and model simplification are needed before clinical implementation as a stand-alone screening tool.

title: Effects of repeated isometric exercise on pain-related and physical recovery outcomes following exercise-induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate repeated quadriceps isometric exercise for recovery following experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes.
DESIGN: Parallel-group, randomized sham-controlled trial.
METHODS: Forty university athletes were randomized to isometric exercise (n = 20) or sham exercise (n = 20). Co-primary outcomes were pressure pain threshold and soreness intensity; secondary outcomes were knee flexion range of motion, quadriceps isometric strength, and thigh circumference. Assessments occurred before and immediately after soreness induction and on Days 1, 3, and 5. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models.
RESULTS: Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for soreness (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.898), pressure pain threshold (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.745), and knee flexion range of motion (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.378). Soreness was lower in the isometric group on Day 1 (mean difference, -2.55 points; 95% confidence interval -3.00 to -2.10; Hedges' g = -3.19) and Day 3 (-1.90 points; 95% confidence interval -2.35 to -1.45; Hedges' g = -2.74). Pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed no significant between-group differences at individual time points. Group × Time interactions were not significant for quadriceps strength or thigh circumference.
CONCLUSIONS: Repeated submaximal isometric exercise was associated with lower perceived soreness during peak symptoms. Although pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed different temporal patterns, neither differed significantly between groups at individual time points. Benefits for physical recovery outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Effects of neuromuscular electrical stimulation applied simultaneously with exercise therapy in patellofemoral pain: A single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simultaneous neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) during exercise may augment task-specific quadriceps activation, but its additional effects in patellofemoral pain (PFP) are uncertain. This pilot trial examined whether adding simultaneous NMES improved pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, quadriceps strength, and muscle thickness compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation.
METHODS: In this single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial, 30 participants were allocated 1:1 to an intervention group or acontrol group. Both groups received the same hip- and knee-targeted exercise therapy twice weekly for 6 weeks. The intervention group received NMES during leg press and leg extension exercises, whereas the control group wore the same device with stimulation intensity set to zero. The primary outcome was worst pain during the previous week, assessed using the visual analogue scale(VAS). Secondary outcomes included the anterior knee pain scale (AKPS), Y-Balance Test (YBT) composite score, isokinetic quadriceps strength (60°/s, 180°/s), and quadriceps muscle thickness.
RESULTS: No additional between-group benefit was detected for worst pain (p = .96; Cohen's d = -0.03), AKPS (p = .26; Cohen's d = -0.24), YBT composite (p = .28; Cohen's d = -0.26), isokinetic strength at 60°/s (p = .67; Cohen's d = -0.11), or 180°/s (p = .56; Cohen's d = -0.12). Total quadriceps muscle thickness increased more in the intervention group than in the control group, but the effect was small (p = .03; Cohen's d = -0.27). No adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSION: No additional short-term benefit of adding simultaneous NMES to exercise therapy was detected for pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, or quadriceps strength compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation. A small increase in total quadriceps muscle thickness was detected, but its clinical relevance remains uncertain. These findings do not support routine addition of simultaneous NMES for short-term pain relief or functional improvement.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Interatrial Septal Disorders are Independently Associated with Delayed Post-Exercise Heart Rate Recovery in Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Interatrial septal disorders (IASD) are among the most common congenital cardiac anomalies. Their impact on cardiac autonomic function in athletes remains poorly defined. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the prevalence of IASD and their association with cardiac autonomic function, assessed by heart rate recovery (HRR), in a cohort of adult athletes.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study enrolled 1,018 adult athletes undergoing pre-participation cardiovascular screening at the Exercise and Sports Medicine Unit of ''A. Cardarelli'' Hospital, Campobasso, Italy, between January 2024 and May 2025. Trans-thoracic echocardiography with contrast imaging was performed to diagnose IASD. HRR was assessed during exercise stress testing using the Modified Bruce Protocol. ΔHRR was calculated as the change from peak heart rate during exercise to that measured during 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th minutes of recovery.
RESULTS: IASD were identified in 331 athletes (32.5%), including patent foramen ovale (12.5%), redundant interatrial septum (21.7%), atrial septal aneurysm (3.3%), and ostium secundum (1.7%). Athletes with IASD exhibited significantly lower ΔHRR at 1 min (30.8 ± 13.9 vs. 39.9 ± 18.1 bpm, p < 0.001) and 2 min (61.0 ± 17.9 vs. 66.1 ± 16.7 bpm, p < 0.001) post-exercise. On multivariable regression, IASD was the strongest independent predictor of impaired ΔHRR 1 (β =- 11.19, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: IASD are prevalent in athletes and independently associated with delayed post-exercise early HRR, suggesting an impairment in post-exercise vagal reactivation.

title: Body recomposition in adults: mechanisms, modulators, and practical algorithms for simultaneous skeletal muscle mass gain and fat mass loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body recomposition is the concurrent increase in fat-free mass (FFM) or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass (FM) within the same intervention period. Although hypertrophy is commonly pursued in energy surplus and FM loss in energy deficit, controlled trials indicate that recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training (PRT), adequate protein intake, and an appropriate energy prescription are combined.
METHODS: We conducted a structured narrative review of randomised trials, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies in adults, with emphasis on FFM, FM, strength, and performance outcomes. Device heterogeneity was considered when interpreting evidence, with greatest weight placed on four-compartment and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcomes.
RESULTS: PRT combined with higher protein intake, typically ~1.6-2.4 g/kg/day and higher relative intakes during energy restriction or leanness, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition. Effects are largest in untrained individuals and those with higher adiposity, smaller in trained or lean athletes, and still feasible in older adults when anabolic resistance is addressed with supervised PRT and sufficient protein. Moderate deficits, carbohydrate allocation around key sessions, sleep, and recovery support FFM retention or accretion while facilitating FM loss. Practical applications: Programmes should pair progressive overload with protein-centred diets, modest energy deficits, and periodic monitoring of body composition and performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Body recomposition is feasible but context-dependent; expected changes are generally modest in trained or lean populations and require individualised adjustment.

title: Neuromuscular performance, physiological recovery, and maturation-referenced reference values in youth athletes: A cross-sectional study.
abstract: This cross-sectional study characterized neuromuscular performance and acute physiological responses across age, sex, and biological maturation in 140 youth athletes (74 boys, 66 girls; 10-16 years), and described maturation-stratified distributions of two field measures. Participants completed 30-m sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), standing long jump (SLJ), and handgrip testing; post-sprint heart-rate recovery (HRrec-30s) and a testing-battery perceived-exertion index (PEI) served as co-primary physiological/perceptual outcomes; maturity offset (Mirwald method) classified Pre-, Circa-, and Post-PHV subgroups; allometric scaling was used to account for body size; and a Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied across a pre-specified family of 58 pairwise comparisons and correlations (Tables 2-6). Boys outperformed girls across all neuromuscular tests (d = 0.63-0.76), whereas HRrec-30s and the perceived-exertion index did not differ significantly by sex. HRrec-30s was more strongly associated with maturity offset than with chronological age (r = 0.52 vs 0.46; η²p for maturation vs age groups 0.43 vs 0.39). Mean HRrec-30s was 27.8 ± 6.2 bpm in the Pre-PHV group and 45.3 ± 8.8 bpm in the Post-PHV group (p < 0.001, FDR-corrected). The perceived-exertion index was lower in more mature groups (7.5 ± 1.2 vs 6.3 ± 1.1). Sex and maturation differences in jump and strength performance remained after allometric scaling, although they were smaller. Maturation-stratified distributions reported here are preliminary and descriptive and are not decision thresholds; prospective, criterion-validated research is needed before they can be recommended for individual athlete monitoring or training-load decision-making.

title: Running Gait Biomechanics Associated With Tibial Bone Stress Injuries Among Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tibial bone stress injuries (BSIs) are common among adolescent runners; however, no studies have evaluated running biomechanics associated with tibial BSI in adolescents.
OBJECTIVE: To describe biomechanical and clinical features among adolescents with a history of tibial BSI, and compare with healthy age- and sex-matched controls.
DESIGN: Retrospective cross-sectional case-control study.
SETTING: Large tertiary-care hospital and affiliated sports injury prevention center.
PARTICIPANTS: Sixty-six adolescents with history of tibial BSI (16.2 ± 1.8 years, BMI: 21.4 ± 3.0 kg/m2) were compared with 66 age- and sex-matched adolescents without a history of tibial BSI (16.3 ± 1.9 years, BMI: 21.7 ± 2.6 kg/m2).
INTERVENTIONS: Medical record review was conducted for tibia BSI case participants. Data from gait analyses completed on an instrumented treadmill.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Participant demographics were compared using independent samples t-tests. Continuous outcome measures [stride length, cadence, %stance phase, and peak mass-normalized vertical ground reaction force (vGRF)], and vertical average load rates (VALR), were compared between groups using independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, with Cohen d effect sizes reported.
RESULTS: Study participants with history of tibial BSI demonstrated increased VALR (μ = 1141, P = 0.01, d = 0.29), increased mass-normalized maximum vGRF (μ = 1657, P = 0.02, d = 0.24), and greater % stance phase (μ = 1392, P < 0.001, d = 0.36).
CONCLUSION: Adolescents with a history of tibial BSI demonstrated characteristic gait biomechanics including greater VALR, greater mass-normalized maximum vGRF, and more terrestrial gait pattern. These features should be considered in management of adolescent tibial BSI.

title: Chlorella intake combined with short-term high-intensity intermittent training further enhances exercise performance in female lacrosse players: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover trial.
abstract: Lacrosse is a fast-paced field sport that requires aerobic, anaerobic, and sprint performance. Chronic Chlorella intake combined with high-intensity intermittent training (HIIT) enhances aerobic, anaerobic, and sprint performance in untrained young adults. This study aimed to clarify the effects of combining Chlorella intake with short-term HIIT on aerobic, anaerobic, and sprint performance in female lacrosse players. In a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial, twelve female collegiate lacrosse players were enrolled, ten participants completed 3 weeks of HIIT, comprising 7 bouts of running at full speed with a 10-second rest between each bout, 5 days/week. They were orally administered Chlorella (CH) or a placebo (PL) for 3-week in a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover design with a 5-week washout period. This study measured the 20-meter shuttle run test (20m SRT) and estimated maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) as indices of aerobic performance, 50-meter sprint time as an index of sprint performance, and the 30-second Wingate test as an index of anaerobic performance. No significant differences by trial or time point were observed in aerobic (20m SRT and VO2max) or anaerobic performance (Wingate test), including 50-meter sprint time. However, improvements were observed in the HIIT + CH trial for most exercise performance outcomes (P < 0.05), but not in the HIIT + PL trial. These exploratory results suggest that CH intake may improve short-term HIIT-induced changes in exercise performance in female lacrosse players, although the small sample size and short intervention period warrant cautious interpretation.

title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Sports-Related Back Pain and Injuries: From Muscle Strain to Spondylolisthesis.
abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. title: Return to sports after pediatric brain tumors: Time to move beyond survival.
abstract: Brain tumors are the second most common malignancy in children and adolescents and the leading cause of cancer-related death in this population. While survival rates have improved, survivors are at risk of neurocognitive, motor, and psychosocial sequelae due to both tumor location and treatments used. Participation in sport is increasingly recognized as beneficial for functional recovery, cardiorespiratory fitness, and overall well-being in children and adolescents treated for brain tumors. However, return to play (RTP) may pose some challenges, particularly in the presence of neurosurgical devices, cranial radiotherapy, or residual neurological deficits. This narrative clinical review summarizes current evidence on the risks of sport-related injuries in pediatric brain tumor patients and survivors, highlighting factors influencing vulnerability, including treatment history and specific sport characteristics. We propose a risk-based framework for RTP evaluation emphasizing individualized coordinated assessment by pediatric oncologists, neurosurgeons, and sports medicine specialists. Protective strategies are discussed, although evidence for concussion prevention remains limited. A safe RTP should be enhanced by the here-proposed structured evaluation, balancing safety with the physical, cognitive, and psychosocial benefits of active participation. This framework aims to support clinicians and families in facilitating safe and effective reintegration of pediatric brain tumor survivors into both recreational and competitive sports.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Editorial Commentary: Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Requires the Right Patient, the Right Dose, and the Right Time.
abstract: Quadriceps weakness is a persistent challenge after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. When used as an adjunct to rehabilitation, neuromuscular electrical stimulation can aid in quadriceps strength recovery. However, optimizing the clinical application of neuromuscular electrical stimulation requires consideration of the right patient, the right dose, and the right time. title: Being treated as more than a diagnosis: A qualitative interview study exploring patients' experiences of physiotherapeutic guidance in the management of tendinopathy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tendinopathy rehabilitation often involves exercise therapy and patient education. However, limited research has explored how patients experience and assign meaning to the guidance through which such care is delivered.
OBJECTIVES: This study aims to explore how adults with tendinopathy experience and make sense of physiotherapeutic guidance in clinical practice.
STUDY DESIGN: This qualitative study adopted a hermeneutic approach and employed semi-structured interviews with 10 patients receiving treatment for tendinopathy across various anatomical regions to explore their experiences of physiotherapeutic guidance throughout treatment.
RESULTS: From the patients' responses, two major themes were identified: "Meaningful guidance is built through trust, recognition, and individualisation" and "Purposeful guidance helps patients understand and manage the condition". Three sub-themes surfaced within each theme, and similar topics were identified among the patients' responses.
CONCLUSIONS: Physiotherapeutic guidance appears to be meaningful when it integrates relational and functional processes. While trust, recognition, and individualisation support patients' engagement, clear explanations and structured guidance facilitate understanding and self-management in daily life.

title: Delayed Extensor Apparatus Reconstruction for Post-Burn Digital Extension Loss in a Pediatric Patient.
abstract: Late sequelae of pediatric hand burns may include occult damage to the digital extensor apparatus beneath healed scar tissue. The digital extensor apparatus is a complex anatomical system composed of interconnected components that function together to produce coordinated finger extension at interphalangeal joints. Injury to this system may remain clinically unrecognized during acute burn management and present later as isolated extension loss despite preserved joint suppleness. We report the case of a 10-year-old girl who presented 2 years after a flame burn involving the dorsum of the left hand with inability to actively extend the index and middle fingers. Clinical examination demonstrated absent active extension at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, whereas passive motion, sensation, and vascularity were preserved. Overlying skin was supple, though scarred and variably pigmented. Radiographs demonstrated mild proximal interphalangeal joint subluxation of the middle finger without other osseous abnormality. Surgical exploration revealed loss of functional continuity of the digital extensor apparatus distally. Delayed reconstruction was performed using an ipsilateral palmaris longus tendon graft to restore coordinated extension. Temporary axial K-wire immobilization was maintained for 2 weeks, followed by structured rehabilitation. At final follow-up, the patient achieved approximately 80% recovery of active extension, enabling writing and functional grasp. This case underscores the importance of early recognition of occult extensor apparatus damage following pediatric hand burns to prevent functional disability. However, delayed reconstruction can still yield meaningful functional recovery when joint mobility and neurovascular integrity are preserved.

title: Effect Of Joint-Angle Configuration on Hamstring Torque-Duration Relationship Parameters and the Etiology of Motor Performance Fatigue.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study examined how hamstring muscle-tendon unit length influences critical torque (CT), work capacity above CT (W'), and the mechanisms of motor performance fatigue during and after repeated maximal voluntary contractions.
METHODS: Twelve healthy men (25 ± 4 years) performed, on separate days, two fatiguing protocols consisting of fifty 3-s maximal isometric knee flexions (2-s rest) at joint-angle configurations expected to produce relatively long (LL) and short (SL) hamstring muscle-tendon unit lengths. Neuromuscular assessments were conducted before, during, and up to 15 min post-exercise. CT and W' were determined from the torque-duration relationship. Peripheral fatigue was evaluated using peak evoked torques (T100), and central fatigue using voluntary activation (VA) derived from the twitch interpolation technique. Linear mixed-effects models and paired t-tests assessed the effects of time and joint-angle configuration.
RESULTS: CT did not differ between LL and SL (p = 0.65), whereas W' was significantly lower at SL than LL (p < 0.001, d = 0.96). MVC torque decreased by ~45% after fatiguing protocols (p < 0.001, η 2p = 0.84), accompanied by reductions in T100 (-22%) and VA (-17). During recovery, VA returned to baseline within 3 min, while T100 remained depressed throughout recovery (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In the knee flexors, short muscle-tendon unit length reduces the capacity to perform work above CT without altering CT or the magnitude and etiology of fatigue. The rapid recovery of voluntary activation alongside persistent peripheral impairment extends current knowledge of recovery kinetics specifically for repeated maximal knee-flexion exercise.

title: Cortical button versus suture anchor fixation in distal biceps tendon repair: a comparison of objective four-plane strength and functional outcomes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare four-plane isometric strength, function and complications between cortical button and suture anchor fixation in distal biceps repair, and to explore the influence of surgical delay.
METHODS: Twenty-eight men (mean age, 44.2 years) underwent single-incision repair with a cortical button (n = 16) or suture anchors (n = 12) between 2020 and 2025. At a mean follow-up of 46 months, we assessed isometric strength in four planes with a hand-held dynamometer (relative to the uninjured side), range of motion, QuickDASH, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score (OES) and complications. A sensitivity analysis included only patients followed for ≥ 24 months.
RESULTS: Mean strength was 93.8% (flexion), 100.1% (extension), 90.3% (supination) and 97.2% (pronation; median, 94.2%); all planes except extension remained below the uninjured side (P ≤ 0.016). Strength did not differ between techniques in any plane, also in the sensitivity analysis. Functional scores were high in both groups, with small differences in favour of suture anchors that should be interpreted with caution (MEPS 100 vs. 95.0, P = 0.022; QuickDASH 1.3 vs. 5.5, P = 0.046; OES 47.4 vs. 43.4, P = 0.069). Repair after 21 days (n = 6; exploratory) was associated with weaker flexion (85.4% vs. 96.1%, P = 0.024). No reruptures occurred; three patients (10.7%) had transient neurapraxia.
CONCLUSION: No significant strength differences were found between techniques, although the small sample cannot exclude clinically relevant differences and fixation was confounded with treatment era. A small supination and flexion deficit persisted after both techniques.

title: Adhesive and Antibacterial Bio-Based Hydrogel for Human Voice Recognition and Osteoarthritis Recovery Monitoring.
abstract: Conductive hydrogels derived from natural polysaccharides hold great promise for next generation wearable electronics owing to their intrinsic biocompatibility, adhesiveness, and tunable mechanical properties. However, realizing amylum-based hydrogels with simultaneously high stretchability, sensitivity, strong adhesion and antibacterial performance remains a significant challenge. Herein, a multifunctional ionic hydrogel, marked as PAPC4 hydrogel, composed of polyacrylamide (PAAm), amylum and phenol-modified chitosan is developed via a one-pot synthesis strategy. The hydrogel exhibits exceptional stretchability (up to 1605%), short response time (16.1 ms), high optical transparency (96%), strong adhesion (43.2 kPa on PVC) and pronounced antibacterial activity. Cytotoxicity assays, live/dead staining, and subcutaneous implantation supported its biocompatibility under the tested conditions, while bacterial assays demonstrated activity against Escherichia coli. As a strain sensor, PAPC4 detected joint movements and throat vibrations during speech. It also recorded differences in knee movement among control, osteoarthritis, and treated osteoarthritis groups in rats. These results support the use of this chitosan-starch composite hydrogel in wearable motion sensing and rehabilitation monitoring.

title: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears in the anterior cruciate ligament-injured knee: Current concepts.
abstract: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears (LMPRTs) compromise load transmission and secondary stability in the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-injured knee and may be missed on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This narrative current-concepts review addresses incidence, risk factors, biomechanics, diagnosis, classification, treatment, and outcomes, while distinguishing root tears from lateral meniscal oblique radial tears (LMORTs). Primary ACL reconstruction (ACLR) cohorts report LMPRT frequencies of 7.1%, 10.0%, and 12.2%; a mixed primary/revision cohort reports 6.6% and selected revision cohorts report 20.5% and 40.7%. These study-specific estimates differ in lesion definition and ascertainment. Contact injury, concomitant medial meniscal pathology, and increased lateral posterior tibial slope are recurring associations. Individual MRI signs have limited sensitivity; combined assessment and arthroscopic inspection and probing support diagnosis. LaPrade et al. describe root-tear morphology, Forkel and Petersen additionally consider meniscofemoral ligament integrity, and LMORT typing describes posterior-horn oblique radial tears. The systems overlap for near-root lesions and are descriptive frameworks rather than validated treatment algorithms. Selected stable lesions may be observed; repairable unstable lesions are generally treated with footprint fixation or side-to-side repair, according to anatomy and tissue quality. Repair with ACLRn is associated with improved patient-reported outcomes and high complete-or-partial healing proportions in selected series. Clinical improvement in ACL graft survivorship has not been demonstrated. Heterogeneous definitions, predominantly lower-level evidence, variable rehabilitation, and limited long-term comparative data, constrain conclusions about cartilage preservation and optimal treatment.

title: A mechanically active microneedle platform integrated with engineered exosomes for enhanced tendon-bone regeneration.
abstract: Functional regeneration of the tendon-bone interface remains a major challenge because early healing is constrained by an adverse inflammatory microenvironment and insufficient mechanical cues. Here, we developed a mechano-regenerative strategy that combines YAP-primed engineered exosomes with localized biomaterial-based delivery and active mechanical stimulation. Exosomes derived from a YAP agonist (PY-60) preconditioned TDSCs (P-Exo) showed enhanced uptake and promoted the osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, accompanied by activation of YAP-associated signaling and PI3K-Akt-related pathways. To improve local retention, P-Exo were incorporated into a ROS-responsive adhesive hydrogel, which accelerated fibrocartilage formation, bone ingrowth, and biomechanical restoration in a rabbit tendon-bone healing model. To address more complex repair conditions, we engineered a three-layer self-contracting microneedle platform for deep-tissue delivery of P-Exo with concurrent active mechanical stimulation. In an infected rat rotator cuff model, this system reduced bacterial burden and oxidative stress, promoted a reparative macrophage polarization and angiogenesis, and improved tendon-bone structural regeneration, biomechanical strength, and functional recovery. Together, these findings support a therapeutic framework in which engineered exosome signaling and active mechanoregulation act in concert to enhance tendon-bone repair.

title: An Adaptive Knee Brace Is Associated With Improved Dynamic Stabilization Compared With a Standard Passive Brace in Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Deficient Men During a Functional Hop Task.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the dynamic knee stabilization effects of an adaptive dynamic brace (ADB) with those of a standard passive brace in anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-deficient men.
METHODS: ACL-deficient participants were included. The subjects performed 3 single-leg functional hop tests: drop jump, crossover hop, and 90° rotational hop. Each task was performed once while wearing the ADB and once while wearing a traditional passive brace. Three-dimensional kinematic data were collected using an 8-camera optoelectronic motion-capture system. Repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to evaluate the effects of brace condition and time. An a priori power analysis indicated that a minimum of 12 participants were required.
RESULTS: Twelve ACL-deficient participants were included (age: 30.2 ± 3.4 years; time since injury: 32 ± 6 months; ACL-Return to Sport after Injury score: 70 ± 3). No significant differences in knee flexion angles were observed between braces. Knee flexion during landing was significantly lower in the crossover hop compared with the drop jump and rotational hop tasks (P < .01). During the drop jump task, the ADB significantly reduced knee valgus angles (P < .01). In the crossover hop task, the ADB significantly reduced both knee valgus and rotational angles (P < .01). During the rotational hop task, a significant brace-by-time interaction was observed for knee valgus (P < .05) and rotational angles (P < .05).
CONCLUSIONS: The ADB showed improved dynamic stabilization particularly during high-risk landing and rotational movement compared with a standard passive brace.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The ADB may enhance the effectiveness of rehabilitation strategies in ACL-deficient individuals by improving dynamic knee stability during functional activities.

title: Obturator internus muscle entrapment in posterior wall acetabular fractures: two cases with preoperative and intraoperative findings.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We report two cases of the rare presentation of obturator internus muscle (OI) entrapment in posterior wall fractures of the acetabulum. Although piriformis muscle entrapment has been previously reported, to the best of our knowledge, OI entrapment associated with posterior wall acetabular fractures has not been previously documented.
CASE PRESENTATION: Case 1: A 38-year-old male presented with right hip and knee pain following a road traffic accident. He was diagnosed with a posterior hip dislocation, posterior wall and posterior column fractures of the acetabulum, and a posterior knee dislocation. During surgery, the OI muscle was found interposed between the displaced posterior wall fragment and the remaining posterior column. Case 2: A 43-year-old male sustained blunt abdominal trauma and a Pipkin type IV injury involving a femoral head fracture associated with a posterior wall acetabular fracture following a road traffic accident. After stabilisation of the abdominal injury with laparoscopic repair of the mesenteric injury, the patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation of the posterior wall fracture, along with removal of intra-articular fragments associated with an infra-foveal femoral head fracture. Intraoperatively, the OI muscle was similarly found interposed between the displaced posterior wall fragment and the remaining posterior column. In both cases, retrospective review of the preoperative CT images demonstrated OI interposition corresponding to the intraoperative findings. Both patients followed a standard postoperative rehabilitation protocol. At the one-year follow-up, both patients had satisfactory clinical outcomes, with Merle d'Aubigné-Postel scores of 16 and 17 and Harris Hip Scores of 92.7 and 93 for Cases 1 and 2, respectively. Neither patient showed radiographic evidence of post-traumatic arthritis.
CONCLUSION: These cases highlight the importance of recognising OI muscle entrapment as a potential cause of difficulty in reducing posterior wall acetabular fractures. Careful evaluation of preoperative CT images, particularly using soft-tissue window settings, may facilitate the identification of OI interposition. Intraoperatively, failure to identify the OI tendon between the superior and inferior gemelli, when both are clearly identified, should raise suspicion of entrapment. Meticulous identification of soft-tissue structures may help achieve anatomical fracture reduction and successful fixation.
